blocks.h: On completing this chapter, the reader should be able to:

items.h: Explain the significance of the claims function as the ultimate test of a life assurance policy and describe the role of claims management in policyholder trust, brand reputation, and regulatory compliance.
Describe the full claims lifecycle, from notification to settlement, and explain the organisational structure and governance of a best-practice life insurance claims function.

Identify and describe the documentation required to support a valid death claim, explain how proof of death is established in different circumstances, and discuss the significance of cause of death in the claims assessment process.

Explain the claims treatment of deaths that are subject to inquest, deaths in disputed or unusual circumstances, missing persons and presumed death, and the operation of the suicide clause in Nigerian life assurance practice.
Describe the claims processes for maturity claims, periodic survival benefits, policy loan repayments, and the settlement of paid-up and surrender values.

Explain the claims requirements and assessment process for accelerated benefit claims, critical illness (CI) and Total and Permanent Disability (TPD), including benefit triggers, survival periods, and waiver of premium provisions.
Describe the fraud risk in Nigerian life assurance claims, identify the key red-flag indicators of fraudulent claims, and explain the insurer’s investigation protocols and available legal remedies.
Explain how claims fraud analytics and automated red-flag systems are used to detect, prioritise, and investigate suspicious claims in a modern Nigerian life insurance operation.
Describe NIIRA 2025’s mandatory claims settlement timeline obligations, policyholder rights on disputed claims, and NAICOM’s enforcement powers in respect of claims payment failures.

Explain the treatment of unclaimed life assurance benefits in Nigeria, the operation of an unclaimed funds registry (a regulatory practice not provided for in the Act), and the appropriate use and governance of ex gratia payments.

blocks.text: 12.1 Introduction: Claims as the Ultimate Test of the Policy

blocks.h: A life insurance policy is a promise. It is a contractual commitment by the insurer to pay a defined sum of money to a defined beneficiary upon the occurrence of a defined event, most commonly the death of the life assured, but also maturity, disability, critical illness, or the periodic survival benefit milestones built into money-back products. Everything else the insurer does (the product design, the underwriting, the premium collection, the investment of reserves) is preparation for the moment when that promise falls due. The claims function is the mechanism through which the promise is either kept or broken.

In the Nigerian insurance market, claims handling has historically been the most significant source of policyholder dissatisfaction and the most powerful contributor to the sector’s poor public perception. Delayed settlements, disputed documentation requirements, arbitrary declinatures, and the disappearance of company records when a claim is presented have all been documented as systemic problems in the pre-NIIRA 2025 era. NAICOM’s consumer protection data consistently showed claims payment failures as the leading category of policyholder complaints.

NIIRA 2025 addresses this history directly. The Act introduces mandatory claims settlement timelines, imposes penalties for non-compliance, gives the claimant recourse to the insurer’s statutory deposit, and reinforces NAICOM’s powers to intervene in claims management failures. These provisions represent the most significant regulatory tightening of the claims function in Nigerian life insurance history.

Beyond compliance, the commercial case for claims excellence is compelling. A life insurance claim typically arrives at one of the most emotionally significant moments in a policyholder family’s life, the death of a breadwinner, a cancer diagnosis, the disability of a parent. The manner in which that claim is handled (the speed, the empathy, the transparency, the professionalism) determines whether the insurer earns lasting trust or permanent enmity. In an era of social media, a poorly handled claim can generate reputational damage that no marketing budget can repair. In an era of mandatory insurance expansion, how the market handles claims determines whether the mandatory policies imposed by NIIRA 2025 become genuine financial protection instruments or mere regulatory compliance exercises.

The claims management function has four core objectives: (a) to assess every claim promptly, fairly, and in accordance with the policy terms and applicable law; (b) to settle valid claims quickly and completely; (c) to identify, investigate, and resist fraudulent claims; and (d) to manage the claims process in a manner that serves the insurer’s duty of good faith to policyholders while protecting the financial interests of the company and its shareholders.

These objectives exist in productive tension. The imperative to settle promptly can conflict with the imperative to investigate thoroughly. The duty of good faith to policyholders can tension with the obligation to resist fraudulent claims. A mature claims function navigates these tensions through clear policies, well-trained staff, defined delegation authorities, and robust governance.

blocks.title: Process: The Life Assurance Claims Lifecycle, Eight Stages

blocks.h: Stage 1: Notification. The claimant (beneficiary, policyholder, or their representative) notifies the insurer of the claim event. Notification may be made in person at a branch, through the agent, by telephone to the customer service centre, or via digital channel. The insurer logs the notification and assigns a claim reference number. Good practice is to acknowledge the notification in writing within 5 business days; this is an internal service standard, because NIIRA 2025 (on the text reviewed) prescribes no acknowledgement period.

Stage 2: Documentation Request. The claims team issues a comprehensive claims checklist specifying all documents required to support the claim. The checklist must be complete and accurate: requesting additional documents at a later stage, ‘goalposts moving’, is a market conduct failure under NIIRA 2025. Documents typically required for a death claim are described in Section 12.3.2.

Stage 3: Document Collection and Verification. Documents submitted by the claimant are reviewed for completeness, authenticity, and internal consistency. Verification checks include: death certificate cross-reference with hospital records; beneficiary identity confirmation against policy schedule; policy in-force status confirmation (premiums paid to date, no lapse); and age at death verification against policy records.

Stage 4: Claims Assessment. The claims officer assesses the claim against the policy terms: is the event an insured event? Is the claimant an eligible beneficiary? Does any policy exclusion apply? Was there material non-disclosure at underwriting that would give the insurer the right to avoid the policy? For contested causes of death, medical evidence is reviewed. For CI and TPD claims, clinical evidence is assessed against policy definitions.

Stage 5: Fraud Triage. Every claim passes through the fraud triage framework (Section 12.8) before approval. Red-flag indicators are automatically or manually checked. Suspicious claims are escalated to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU) before payment is authorised.

Stage 6: Decision and Communication. The claims officer decides to approve, partially approve, or decline the claim. The decision (with clear, written reasons) is communicated to the claimant. Where approved, the payment process is initiated. Where declined, the claimant’s right to dispute the decision and the process for doing so are clearly stated.

Stage 7: Payment. Approved claims are paid through the company’s disbursement system to the verified bank account of the beneficiary. The NIIRA 2025 mandatory settlement period runs for 60 days from notification of the claim (see Section 12.9). Payment confirmation is issued to the beneficiary.

Stage 8: Reinsurance Recovery. Where the claim triggers a reinsurance recovery, the cedant insurer notifies the reinsurer in accordance with the treaty loss notification requirements and submits the recovery claim. Reinsurance recovery is a separate process from policyholder payment; the insurer pays the beneficiary in full and then recovers from the reinsurer under the treaty terms.

blocks.text: 12.2.3 Organisational Structure of the Claims Function

blocks.h: Best-practice claims management requires a dedicated claims function with clear internal structure, defined delegation authorities, and independence from the sales and distribution functions. A life insurance company operating individual, group, and bancassurance lines should structure its claims operation with the following components:

items.h: Claims Operations Team: First-line claims intake, document collection, standard death and maturity claim processing. Handles the high-volume, lower-complexity claims.

Technical Claims Team: Complex death claims, CI and TPD assessments, contestable claims, inquest deaths, and cases involving non-disclosure disputes. Staffed by senior claims officers with medical or legal training.

Special Investigations Unit (SIU): Fraud investigation. The SIU operates independently of the claims approval function; it investigates suspicious claims and reports findings to the Head of Claims and, where appropriate, to the insurer’s legal function and law enforcement agencies.
Group Claims Team: Processing of group life scheme claims, which have distinct documentation requirements and often involve employer intermediation.
Claims Finance and Recoveries: Payment processing, reinsurance recovery management, unclaimed benefit monitoring, and financial reporting on the claims reserve.

blocks.h: A death claim is initiated when the insurer receives notification that the life assured has died. Under most Nigerian life policies, the beneficiary or the policyholder’s estate has an obligation to notify the insurer of the death within a defined period, typically 90 to 180 days. NIIRA 2025 does not extinguish the right to claim because of late notification where the delay is attributable to circumstances beyond the claimant’s reasonable control; however, late notification may complicate the evidence-gathering process and should be addressed promptly once the beneficiary becomes aware of the policy.

On receipt of notification, the claims team should: acknowledge the notification in writing within 5 business days; confirm that the policy is in the insurer’s records and is in force (or lapsed, with confirmation of any lapse benefit payable); assign a claim reference number; and issue the full claims documentation checklist without delay.

Proof of death is the evidentiary foundation of every death claim. In the vast majority of cases, a death certificate issued by the Nigerian National Population Commission (NPC) or the relevant local government authority, together with a hospital medical certificate of cause of death, constitutes sufficient proof. However, a range of circumstances in the Nigerian context creates evidentiary complications that the claims function must be equipped to handle:

Deaths in remote areas: Deaths occurring in rural areas where the deceased was not registered with a healthcare facility, and where NPC registration capacity is limited, may not generate a formal hospital-issued death certificate. In these cases, additional evidence (a declaration by community leaders, a religious leader’s burial certificate, witness statements) may be required and considered alongside whatever official documentation is available.

Deaths abroad: Deaths of Nigerians occurring outside Nigeria require foreign death certificates authenticated by the Nigerian consulate or embassy in the relevant country, together with official translation where the certificate is in a language other than English.

Unidentified remains: Where identification of the deceased’s body has been difficult (mass casualty events, severe decomposition), DNA evidence, dental records, or official coroner identification may be required in addition to or in lieu of a standard death certificate.

Conflict-related deaths: Deaths attributable to armed conflict, communal violence, or terrorist activity present both evidentiary and policy coverage challenges. The insurer must assess whether any policy exclusion for war, military service, or civil unrest is applicable, and must seek whatever official documentation (police, military, or coroner) is available.

blocks.text: 12.3.4 Cause of Death and Its Significance

blocks.h: The recorded cause of death is material to the claims assessment for several reasons. First, it determines whether any policy exclusion applies: most Nigerian life policies exclude death from war and military service; some older policies exclude accidental death under specific circumstances; and aviation exclusions apply to some policies. Second, cause of death is the primary indicator for suicide clause assessment (see Section 12.4.3). Third, for policies with accidental death benefit (ADB) riders, establishing that death was accidental (rather than from natural causes) is the prerequisite for the additional benefit.

Where the stated cause of death on the certificate raises coverage questions, the claims team may seek additional medical evidence: hospital admission records, post-mortem report, attending physician statement, or specialist opinion. The claims officer must assess this evidence objectively and communicate clearly with the claimant about the basis for any decision.

blocks.text: 12.4 Inquest, Disputed Deaths, and the Suicide Clause

blocks.h: An inquest is a formal legal inquiry conducted by a coroner into the cause of death where the death is sudden, unexplained, violent, suspicious, or occurred in custody. In Nigeria, coronial jurisdiction is exercised under the Coroners’ Law applicable in each state. Where a death is the subject of an inquest, the insurer will typically await the coroner’s verdict before finalising its claims assessment, since the inquest may establish facts material to the coverage decision (cause of death, whether the death was accidental or intentional, whether third-party liability is implicated).

The insurer should acknowledge the claim and maintain open communication with the claimant during the inquest period. If the inquest is likely to be prolonged, the insurer should consider making an interim payment of an undisputed portion of the benefit to address immediate hardship, a practice that NIIRA 2025’s good faith obligations would support, and that NAICOM’s market conduct supervisors view favourably.

A missing person is not legally dead until a court grants a declaration of presumed death or a certificate of presumption of death is issued under applicable Nigerian law. Life assurance policies cannot be claimed on the basis of a missing person alone; the beneficiary must obtain a legal declaration before the insurer can pay.

The relevant legislative framework in Nigeria is primarily the Evidence Act 2011, which allows the court to presume death after a person has been continuously absent and unheard of for seven years, if all due inquiries have been made. Some states have specific missing persons legislation. The waiting period creates real hardship for beneficiary families, and insurers should proactively assist claimants in understanding the legal process and, where appropriate, referring them to legal aid organisations.

Where the missing person’s disappearance occurred in circumstances consistent with likely death (a maritime accident, a plane crash where the body was not recovered, a conflict-related disappearance) the court may be satisfied to issue the declaration on a shorter timeline. Insurers should not use the presumed death process as a delay tactic where the circumstances of disappearance make death near-certain; such conduct would likely attract NAICOM regulatory scrutiny under NIIRA 2025.

A policy provision that excludes the insurer’s liability for death by suicide occurring within a defined exclusion period from the policy start date, typically the first 12 to 24 months. After the exclusion period has elapsed, the full sum assured is payable regardless of the cause of death, including suicide. The rationale is to prevent the purchase of life insurance immediately in contemplation of suicide to benefit dependants.

Suicide clauses are standard in Nigerian life assurance policies. The exclusion period varies by insurer, most apply a 12-month exclusion, some use 24 months. Where the death occurs within the exclusion period and is determined to be suicide, the insurer’s liability is typically limited to the return of premiums paid, rather than the full sum assured. After the exclusion period, the full benefit is payable.

Claims assessment under the suicide clause requires objective and sensitive handling. The insurer must establish, on the balance of probabilities, that the death was by suicide rather than accident or other cause. Evidence considered includes: coroner’s findings; police report; medical examination findings; witness statements; and the deceased’s circumstances and behaviour in the period prior to death. The standard of proof is the civil standard (balance of probabilities), not the criminal standard (beyond reasonable doubt). Where the cause of death is genuinely uncertain between suicide and accident, the insurer should resolve the uncertainty in favour of the claimant, consistent with the principle of contra proferentem (ambiguity in policy terms construed against the insurer).

blocks.text: 12.5 Maturity Claims, Survival Benefits, and Policy Loans

blocks.h: A maturity claim arises when an endowment or savings-type policy reaches the end of its defined policy term and the life assured is still alive. The insurer becomes obligated to pay the maturity sum assured (plus any accumulated bonuses, in the case of a with-profit policy) to the policyholder.

Best-practice maturity claims handling involves proactive notification: the insurer should contact the policyholder no less than 90 days before the policy maturity date to confirm their payment details, obtain updated identity documents, and prepare for timely settlement. Policies that are allowed to reach maturity without prior contact risk unclaimed benefit status (see Section 12.10).

Documentation for maturity claims: completed maturity claim form; original policy document; proof of identity; current bank account details for payment. Where a policy loan has been taken against the policy, the outstanding loan balance (principal plus accrued interest) is deducted from the maturity benefit before payment. This deduction and its basis must be clearly communicated to the policyholder in writing.

Money-back plans (periodic endowments) provide for the payment of defined percentages of the sum assured at defined intervals during the policy term, with the balance payable at maturity or on earlier death. These periodic payments are survival benefits: they are payable only if the life assured is alive on the payment date.

The claims process for a survival benefit payment is administratively simpler than a death claim but requires the insurer to maintain accurate policy anniversary records and initiate payment proactively on the anniversary date. Relying on the policyholder to make a formal claim for each scheduled survival benefit is poor practice and creates unclaimed benefit risk. Modern policy administration systems (PAS) should generate automatic payment instructions for all scheduled survival benefit payments, subject only to confirmation that the premium account is current.

A policy loan is not technically a claim; it is a contractual right of the policyholder to borrow against the accumulated surrender value of the policy up to a defined percentage (typically 80–90% of the current surrender value). The loan does not require proof of insurability, credit assessment, or lender approval; it is a self-secured advance against the policyholder’s own accumulated value.

From a claims perspective, policy loans are relevant because: outstanding loan balances (principal and accrued interest) are deducted from the sum payable on death, maturity, or surrender; a policy loan that is not serviced will, if the accrued interest exceeds the available policy value, cause the policy to lapse, creating a claims denial issue if the policyholder dies in a lapsed state without appreciating the lapse. The insurer’s obligation to communicate policy loan account status proactively to policyholders is both a contractual and a consumer protection obligation.

A policyholder who wishes to terminate their policy before maturity may either surrender the policy for its cash surrender value, or convert to a paid-up policy (where future premiums cease but the policy remains in force for a reduced sum assured, with no further premium obligation). Both involve a claims-like process: the policyholder submits a request, the claims or policy servicing team calculates the applicable value, and payment or conversion is effected.

Surrender values are calculated by the actuary as the present value of future policy benefits less future expenses and a surrender penalty (if applicable), reflecting the front-loaded cost structure of life insurance products. Policyholders who surrender in the early years of a long-term policy typically receive significantly less than their total premium contributions, a fact that must be communicated clearly in the policy terms and benefit illustration. NIIRA 2025’s consumer protection provisions require surrender value terms to be clearly disclosed at point of sale and in the policy document.

A critical illness (CI) benefit pays a lump sum upon the policyholder’s diagnosis with one of the defined dread diseases listed in the policy schedule. The most commonly covered conditions in Nigerian CI products include: cancer (specified stages and types); myocardial infarction (heart attack); stroke resulting in permanent neurological deficit; kidney failure requiring permanent dialysis; coronary artery bypass surgery; major organ transplant; aortic surgery; and blindness.
The claims assessment for CI benefits involves three key determinations:

Confirm the condition meets the policy’s clinical definition. Dread disease definitions are precise, a ‘heart attack’ claim must meet the policy’s specific criteria for myocardial infarction (enzyme levels, ECG changes, symptoms).

blocks.h: Where the CI benefit is structured as an ‘accelerated benefit’ (a deduction from the life sum assured rather than an addition), the outstanding life cover is reduced by the amount of the CI payment, and the life assurance premium may be correspondingly reduced. The policyholder must be clearly advised of the impact of the CI payment on the remaining life benefit before settlement is completed.

Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) is defined in life assurance policies as a condition in which the policyholder is, as a result of injury or illness, permanently unable to engage in any occupation for which they are reasonably qualified by education, training, or experience, or, in some policy definitions, their own specific occupation. TPD claims are among the most complex and contested in life assurance practice because:

items.h: The definition of ‘permanent’ is clinically uncertain: many disabling conditions have a degree of recovery potential that makes an early declaration of permanence difficult.

The definition of ‘total’ is contested: a policyholder who is disabled from their specific occupation but can undertake some other form of work may not meet the ‘any occupation’ definition in the policy.
The assessment requires medical, functional capacity, and often vocational expert opinion, creating a multi-disciplinary claims process that is both resource-intensive and time-consuming.

blocks.h: Best practice for TPD claims assessment includes: early engagement of an independent medical examiner familiar with functional capacity assessment; clear communication with the claimant about the assessment process and timeline; and a defined review period for cases where the medical evidence of permanence is not yet conclusive.

TPD benefit payments under NIIRA 2025 are subject to the same mandatory settlement timelines as death claims (once the assessment is complete and all evidence received). Indefinite deferral of a TPD assessment is not acceptable.

A waiver of premium rider provides that, upon the policyholder’s total disability, the insurer waives (does not require payment of) the policy premium during the period of disability, keeping the policy in force without cost to the disabled policyholder. The assessment criteria are similar to TPD, but the waiver applies to temporary total disability as well as permanent disability in many product designs.

Claims management for waiver of premium requires ongoing monitoring: the waiver applies only while the disability continues, so the claims team must conduct periodic reassessments (typically annually) to confirm that the disability criteria are still met. If the policyholder recovers and returns to work, premium payment resumes from the date of recovery. This ongoing case management obligation is an important operational responsibility that requires dedicated tracking within the claims administration system.

blocks.text: 12.7.1 The Fraud Problem in Nigerian Life Insurance

blocks.h: Claims fraud is a material financial risk in the Nigerian life insurance market. Industry estimates, consistent with international actuarial survey data, suggest that between 5% and 15% of claims value in some product lines may involve some element of fraud or misrepresentation, a range that, applied to the total life industry claims payout, represents a substantial annual financial loss. Fraud directly erodes the profitability of the claims function, inflates premiums for honest policyholders, and, in the worst cases, destabilises the financial position of smaller insurers.
Nigerian life insurance fraud takes several forms. The most common patterns encountered by the industry include:

items.h: False death claims: A claim is submitted for a death that did not occur, with fabricated or forged death certificates, medical records, and identity documents. The ‘deceased’ may be living and complicit, or the entire claim may be an identity fraud. This is the most serious and most prevalent category of life claims fraud in Nigeria.

Non-disclosure fraud at underwriting: The proposer conceals a pre-existing medical condition at underwriting, paying premiums on a policy they know they could not obtain or could only obtain at a loaded rate. When the pre-existing condition causes death or disability, a claim is submitted. This is distinguishable from innocent non-disclosure by the degree of deliberateness and the relevance of the undisclosed condition to the claim.

Staging and opportunistic fraud: Legitimate policyholders exaggerate the severity of a genuine condition (particularly in CI and TPD claims) to ensure the claim meets the policy’s benefit trigger. A genuine but mild cardiac event may be documented as a ‘heart attack’ meeting the policy’s myocardial infarction definition when it technically does not.

Agent-facilitated fraud: Agents assist proposers to complete proposal forms in a manner that conceals material information, or submit claims on behalf of policyholders with fabricated documentation. Agent involvement transforms a policyholder fraud into an organised fraud scheme, requiring a different investigation response.

Syndicate fraud: Organised crime groups systematically purchase life insurance policies (using false identities or recruits), pay premiums for the minimum period before a claim, and then submit fraudulent death or CI claims. Syndicate fraud is characterised by patterns across multiple policies with common beneficiaries, addresses, or bank accounts.

blocks.title: Claims Fraud Red-Flag Indicators: Apply to All Claims

blocks.h: The following indicators do not establish fraud but require heightened scrutiny and escalation to the SIU:
POLICY-LEVEL INDICATORS

items.h: Death or disability occurring very shortly after policy issue (within the first 6–12 months), particularly where the policy was taken out near the maximum non-medical limit.
Multiple policies on the same life held with different insurers, aggregate sum assured significantly exceeds income multiple limits.
Policy was taken out following the insured’s diagnosis of a serious illness (suggesting undisclosed pre-existing condition).
Policy premium was paid by a third party who is also the beneficiary, with no evident insurable interest relationship.

blocks.h: DOCUMENTATION INDICATORS

items.h: Death certificate from an issuing authority inconsistent with the deceased’s known place of residence.
Discrepancies between the cause of death on the death certificate and the cause on the hospital records or attending physician statement.
Alterations, corrections, or signs of tampering on submitted documents.
Death certificate issued unusually quickly after the stated date of death; or issued long after, with no explanation for the delay.
Hospital name on records is not registered or not located at the stated address.

blocks.h: CLAIMANT BEHAVIOUR INDICATORS

items.h: Claimant is unusually knowledgeable about the exact policy terms, sum assured, and documentation requirements.
Claimant is uncooperative with reasonable requests for additional verification or interview.
Beneficiary bank account was recently opened (within 30 days of the claim notification).
Multiple claimants on different policies providing the same beneficiary bank account details.

blocks.h: PATTERN INDICATORS

items.h: The same agent submitted the policy and is now actively managing the claim, with unusually detailed involvement in the documentation process.
Multiple claims from the same geographic area, employer, or beneficiary network within a short period, potential syndicate indicator.
The same witness signature appears on multiple claim documents for different policyholders.

blocks.h: Where red-flag indicators are present, the claim is escalated to the Special Investigations Unit (SIU). The SIU investigation protocol includes the following steps:

items.h: Initial review: The SIU officer reviews all available file documentation, cross-references the policy records, and assesses which specific indicators are present. A preliminary investigation scope is defined.

Document verification: Documents are submitted for independent authentication, death certificates cross-referenced with the National Population Commission database; hospital records cross-referenced with the hospital directly; identity documents cross-referenced with NIMC or relevant issuing authority.

Field investigation: For serious fraud suspicion, a field investigator (in-house or contracted) visits the stated address of the deceased, the hospital, and the beneficiary. In Nigeria, field investigation is a critical and irreplaceable component of fraud detection: document forgery that survives paper scrutiny is often quickly exposed by a visit to the stated location.

Claimant interview: A structured interview with the claimant, conducted by the SIU officer, to establish facts and identify inconsistencies. Claimants must be informed that the interview is part of the fraud investigation process.
Medical review: For CI, TPD, and medical-evidence-dependent death claims, an independent medical officer reviews the submitted clinical records for authenticity and medical plausibility.

blocks.h: The insurer must maintain the claim within the NIIRA 2025 mandatory settlement timeline during the investigation. Where the investigation requires time beyond the standard settlement period, the insurer must notify the claimant of the investigation and the expected timeline, in writing. NAICOM-supervised insurers may be required to report fraud investigation cases to NAICOM on request.
Where fraud is established, the insurer’s options include:

items.h: Policy avoidance: Where fraud arises from material non-disclosure at underwriting (the proposer knowingly concealed a relevant health condition), the insurer has the right to avoid the policy ab initio, to treat it as if it never existed. The effect is that no benefit is payable. In cases of innocent non-disclosure, avoidance may not be available; the insurer may only be entitled to adjust the claim to what it would have been had the true information been provided at underwriting.

Claim denial with written reasons: Where the claim is fraudulent but the policy itself was validly issued, the claim is denied with written reasons. NIIRA 2025 requires all declinations to include the specific grounds for the decision.
Civil action for recovery: Where a fraudulent claim has already been paid before the fraud was discovered, the insurer may pursue civil recovery proceedings against the fraudulent claimant.

Criminal referral: Fraud in insurance documents is an offence under the Criminal Code Act and the Insurance Act. Serious fraud cases (particularly syndicate fraud, forgery of official documents, or fraud involving company employees or agents) should be reported to the Nigeria Police Force and/or the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC). Criminal referrals serve both justice and deterrence functions.

Agent/intermediary sanctions: Where agent facilitation is established, the insurer should terminate the agency agreement and report the agent to NAICOM and the NIA for regulatory action and potential deregistration.

blocks.text: 12.8 Claims Fraud Analytics and Red-Flag Systems

blocks.h: Manual red-flag checking by individual claims officers is a necessary but insufficient fraud control for a life insurer processing significant volumes of claims. As claim volumes grow and fraud networks become more sophisticated, technology-enabled fraud analytics are essential to maintain the effectiveness of the fraud detection function without imposing unsustainable manual review burdens.
A modern life insurance fraud analytics framework comprises three components: a rules engine, a statistical anomaly detection system, and a case management platform.

rows: Component
Function
Nigerian Implementation Considerations
Rules Engine

Applies a set of predefined business rules to every claim at intake. Each rule corresponds to a known fraud indicator. Claims that trigger one or more rules are flagged for enhanced review, with the number and severity of triggered rules determining the escalation level.

Rules are derived from the insurer’s own fraud history and from NIA industry fraud data. Initial rules implementation typically covers 15–25 rules. Rules are reviewed quarterly and updated as new fraud patterns emerge.
Statistical Anomaly Detection

Uses historical claims data to build a model of ‘normal’ claims patterns. Individual claims that deviate from normal patterns in multiple dimensions simultaneously (e.g., unusual combination of policy age, sum assured, cause of death, and beneficiary account opening date) are flagged, even if no single factor triggers a specific rule.

Requires a claims data history of sufficient size to train the model (typically 2–3 years of claims data with confirmed fraud labels). Nigerian insurers in the early stages of analytics implementation may rely more heavily on rules-based systems while accumulating training data.
Case Management Platform

A dedicated system for tracking fraud investigation cases from initial flag through to resolution, maintaining all investigation documentation and audit trail. Integrates with the claims processing system to ensure flagged claims are not paid until investigation is resolved.

Many Nigerian life insurers currently manage fraud cases through Excel or manual files. Migration to a dedicated case management platform, whether a standalone fraud tool or a module within the PAS, is a priority investment for insurers seeking to systematise their fraud function.

blocks.h: Industry collaboration is a particularly powerful tool for Nigerian life fraud detection. Fraud syndicates operate across multiple insurers: a policy-and-claim pattern that no single insurer’s data can identify as abnormal may be immediately obvious in an industry-wide database. The Nigerian Insurers Association (NIA) operates a Claims Register and a fraud information-sharing platform; active participation in NIA industry data systems should be treated as a non-negotiable operational standard, not an optional add-on.

blocks.text: 12.9 NIIRA 2025: Mandatory Claims Settlement Timelines and Policyholder Rights

blocks.h: NIIRA 2025 introduces, for the first time in Nigerian insurance law, explicit statutory timelines for life assurance claims settlement. These provisions are among the most commercially significant in the Act for the claims function, because they create directly enforceable policyholder rights backed by NAICOM regulatory penalties.

Settlement Timeline: Under s.210 of NIIRA 2025 the insurer must settle a valid claim, pay the benefit, within 60 days of notification of the claim, or such shorter period as NAICOM may prescribe. The same statutory period applies to individual life and group life claims. Insurers should set shorter internal targets so that the statutory period is never approached.

Interest on Late Payment: Claims not settled within the mandatory timeline attract compound interest on the outstanding amount for each month of delay (s.210 NIIRA 2025). The insurer is also liable to a penalty of ₦500,000 (s.210(7)); the claimant may ask NAICOM to pay an unpaid claim from the insurer’s statutory deposit (s.210(2)); and for compulsory insurances s.210(8) allows compensation for unreasonable delay. This eliminates the financial advantage of deliberate delay.

Acknowledgement Standard: Insurers should acknowledge every claims notification in writing within 5 business days. This is recommended practice and an internal service standard; no statutory acknowledgement period has been confirmed in NIIRA 2025.

Documentation Obligation: The insurer must issue a complete claims documentation checklist at the time of acknowledgement. Requesting documents not included in the initial checklist after the claimant has begun document gathering is prohibited except where new information becomes available that legitimately requires additional evidence.

Dispute Resolution: Where a claim is declined or disputed, the claimant has the right to: (a) request an internal review by the insurer’s senior management; (b) refer the dispute to NAICOM’s Consumer Protection Department; and (c) pursue the matter through the courts or Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) mechanisms. The insurer must inform claimants of these rights in every declination letter.

NAICOM Enforcement: NAICOM has authority under NIIRA 2025 to impose administrative sanctions on insurers with systematic claims payment failures, including financial penalties, publication of non-compliance records, and, in extreme cases, suspension of the insurer’s licence to write new business.

The practical implications for claims operations are significant. The 60-day settlement clock creates an absolute deadline that must be tracked for every claim in the system. Insurers must invest in claims management systems capable of: automatically calculating the documentation-complete date for each claim; tracking the settlement deadline for each case; generating management alerts when claims approach the deadline; and producing NAICOM-compliant reports on settlement performance.

Fraud investigations present a specific tension with the mandatory timeline. Where a claim is under SIU investigation, the insurer cannot simply pause the clock. Best practice is to: communicate promptly with the claimant about the investigation status; where possible, pay any undisputed portion of the benefit within the timeline; and if a full investigation requires more time, document the grounds for delay and maintain ongoing communication with the claimant. NAICOM guidance on this issue distinguishes between legitimate, documented investigation delay and abusive delay designed to avoid payment.

blocks.text: 12.10 Unclaimed Benefits and the Unclaimed Funds Registry

blocks.h: Unclaimed benefits are matured, lapsed, or deceased-claimant policy benefits that the insurer is unable to pay because it cannot locate the policyholder or beneficiary. They represent both a financial liability (the insurer holds funds that belong to policyholders or their estates) and a governance risk (unclaimed funds can mask poor operational practices and create regulatory liability).

The scale of unclaimed benefits in the Nigerian life market is significant. Policies that were taken out decades ago, premium payments that stopped being recorded when the collecting agent left, endowment policies whose maturity date passed without the policyholder being located; these are systemic features of a market where customer record quality has historically been poor and portfolio management systems have been fragmented.

A central repository established under NIIRA 2025, administered by NAICOM, to which life insurers are required to remit life assurance benefit proceeds that have remained unclaimed for a defined period (typically three to five years after the benefit fell due). The Registry maintains records of all remitted amounts by policy number, policyholder name, and sum assured, and provides a mechanism through which rightful claimants can search for and recover unclaimed funds.
The key obligations imposed on insurers in relation to unclaimed benefits under NIIRA 2025 are:

items.h: Proactive tracing: Before classifying a benefit as unclaimed, the insurer must make documented efforts to contact the policyholder or beneficiary, by post to the last known address, by phone to the last known number, by email, and through the agent who wrote the policy.
Annual reporting: Insurers must report all unclaimed benefit amounts to NAICOM annually, in the prescribed format, as part of the statutory regulatory returns.

Remittance [practice under NAICOM rules, not found in NIIRA 2025; confirm the source before relying on it]: Funds that remain unclaimed after the prescribed period must be remitted to the Unclaimed Funds Registry. The insurer’s obligation to the policyholder or estate does not extinguish; when a rightful claimant is identified, the insurer remains responsible for recovering the funds from the Registry and paying the beneficiary.
Publication: Insurers are required to publish lists of unclaimed benefits in at least two national newspapers annually, as a public tracing mechanism.

blocks.h: The Unclaimed Funds Registry also serves a market integrity function: it prevents the inadvertent absorption of policyholder funds into an insurer’s operating income, a practice that, if prevalent, would represent a significant consumer harm. Regulators in other African markets (Kenya, South Africa) with similar registries have found that a significant proportion of ‘unclaimed’ funds are ultimately claimed once systematic tracing and publication efforts are applied.

A payment made by the insurer to a claimant as a gesture of goodwill, without legal obligation and without admission of liability. An ex gratia payment does not create a precedent for future claims and does not constitute an acknowledgement that the policy terms required a payment to be made.
Ex gratia payments arise in the following circumstances in life assurance practice:

items.h: Borderline claim decisions: Where a claim strictly fails to meet the policy’s technical requirements (for example, a CI claim where the clinical evidence just falls short of the policy definition, or a death claim where the exclusion is technically applicable but the circumstances are sympathetic) an ex gratia payment may be made to avoid a harsh outcome and preserve the relationship with the policyholder’s family.

Operational failure: Where the insurer’s own administrative failure contributed to the policyholder’s adverse outcome (for example, where an erroneous lapse notice caused the policyholder to believe their policy was in force when it was not) an ex gratia payment acknowledges the insurer’s operational responsibility.

Hardship and vulnerability: Where the claimant is in extreme financial hardship, is elderly, is a minor, or is otherwise vulnerable, the insurer may exercise discretion to make a payment that the strict policy terms do not require, as an expression of corporate responsibility.

blocks.h: Ex gratia payments must be governed by a formal policy and approval framework. The potential for abuse (ex gratia payments being used to avoid a proper fraud investigation, or to settle claims that should properly be declined in the interest of the honest policyholder pool) requires that every ex gratia payment be approved at a senior management level (typically by the Head of Claims in consultation with the Chief Executive or Board Claims Committee), documented with clear reasoning, and reported in the claims management information as a separate category.

NIIRA 2025 does not prohibit ex gratia payments but subjects them to the insurer’s overall duty of treating customers fairly and its obligation to avoid practices that could constitute an implicit admission of systematic claims mis-management.

blocks.text: 12.12 Advisory: Claims Management Best Practices for Nigerian Life Insurers

blocks.h: This section is directed at claims directors, senior operations managers, and Board members responsible for claims governance. It sets out the operational and strategic reforms that distinguish a best-in-class claims function from a compliant-but-mediocre one.

Measurement is the foundation of improvement. Life insurers that do not systematically track their claims performance cannot manage it. The following KPI framework is recommended for the Nigerian life insurance claims function:

rows: Average Claims Settlement Time (individual life)
Target: < 25 days from receipt of complete documentation. NIIRA 2025 mandatory maximum: 60 days. Measure monthly by product type.
Average Claims Settlement Time (group life)
Target: < 45 days from notification. NIIRA 2025 mandatory maximum: 60 days (the same period as individual life).
Claims Documentation Completeness Rate

Percentage of claims where all required documents are received with the initial submission (without a supplementary request). Target: > 70%. Low rates indicate inadequate distribution-channel claims education.
Claims Repudiation (Declination) Rate
Total declined claims as a percentage of all claims received. Track by product type and distribution channel. Unexplained increases may indicate fraud surge or underwriting quality deterioration.
Fraud Detection Rate

Percentage of claims that trigger fraud investigation. The proportion ultimately confirmed as fraudulent gives the ‘hit rate’, a measure of fraud detection accuracy. Target hit rate: > 40% of SIU referrals.
Ex Gratia Payment Rate
Ex gratia payments as a percentage of total claims paid. High rates may indicate systemic policy wording problems; low rates consistently over time may indicate overly rigid claims handling.
Interest Penalties Incurred
Amount of NIIRA 2025 late-payment interest penalties paid. A non-zero figure requires root cause analysis. Any penalty paid to a regulator must be reported to the Board.
Customer Satisfaction Score (Claims)
Post-claims survey of claimants on their experience of the claims process. Target: > 75% satisfied or very satisfied. Segmented by approval vs. declined claims.
Reinsurance Recovery Efficiency
Time from claim payment to reinsurance recovery receipt. Long recovery periods affect cash flow and indicate treaty administration weaknesses.

blocks.h: The traditional adversarial model of life assurance claims handling (in which the insurer treats every claimant with suspicion until the claim is proved) is commercially and ethically outdated. The overwhelming majority of life insurance claims are valid claims from grieving families who have suffered a genuine loss. The claims experience for these claimants shapes the family’s lifetime relationship with insurance.
Claimant-centred claims handling is built on four principles:

items.h: Empathy first: All initial claim interactions are conducted with acknowledgement of the claimant’s circumstances. Staff who handle death claims must receive specific training in communicating with bereaved families, a skill distinct from general customer service skills.

Transparency always: Claimants receive clear, plain-language communication about what documents are needed, why, and the timeline for their claim. If a claim is being investigated, the claimant is told this, in general terms, without compromising the investigation. If a claim is declined, the reasons are stated in plain language, not in policy jargon designed to obscure the basis for the decision.

Proactive case management: The claims officer assigned to a case takes ownership of it, proactively chasing outstanding documents, following up on medical evidence requests, and providing the claimant with progress updates at defined intervals (at least every 10 business days for open cases). Claimants should not need to chase the insurer for a status update.

Genuine fairness: The claims decision is based on the actual policy terms and applicable law, applied consistently. Policies are interpreted in good faith. Ambiguities are resolved in favour of the claimant. Technical defences are not deployed in circumstances where the practical justice of the claim is clear.

blocks.text: 12.12.3 Technology and Automation in Claims Management

blocks.h: Digital transformation of the claims function is a competitive necessity in the Nigerian market. Insurers whose claims processes remain paper-dependent face structural disadvantages in speed, accuracy, fraud detection, and regulatory compliance tracking.
Priority technology investments for the Nigerian life insurance claims function include:

items.h: Claims management system (CMS) integration with PAS: Every claim should be directly linked to the policy record in the PAS, enabling automatic policy status verification, premium payment history retrieval, and beneficiary confirmation at claim intake.

Digital document submission: A secure digital portal or email-based submission channel for claims documentation, with automatic OCR (optical character recognition) to extract key data fields for the claims record.

Automated eligibility checking: Automated system checks at claim intake: policy in force on date of claim event; sum assured; beneficiary details; applicable exclusions. These checks, which take a claims officer 15–20 minutes manually, can be completed in seconds by an integrated system.

Settlement timeline tracker: An automatically managed countdown clock for every active claim, tracking the NIIRA 2025 settlement deadline and generating escalation alerts when claims are at risk of breaching the timeline.
Fraud analytics integration: Rules engine and anomaly detection outputs feeding automatically into the claims workflow, flagging suspicious claims before they reach the payment queue.

blocks.h: Reinsurance recoveries are a material cash flow item for Nigerian life insurers with significant group life and large individual life portfolios. The discipline of recoveries management is frequently under-resourced relative to its financial importance.

Best-practice reinsurance recoveries management involves: immediate loss advice to the reinsurer upon notification of a large claim (consistent with treaty loss reporting requirements, typically 100% of the policy value); prompt submission of the formal recovery claim with complete documentation upon policy payment; active monitoring of recovery timelines against the treaty’s payment schedule; and escalation to senior management when recoveries are delayed beyond treaty terms.

blocks.title: Advisory: Reinsurance Recovery, Common Failures in Nigerian Practice

blocks.h: The following operational failures in reinsurance recoveries management are commonly observed among Nigerian direct insurers and carry significant cash flow and financial reporting risk:

items.h: Failure to notify the reinsurer of large claims within the treaty’s required notification window, creating grounds for the reinsurer to dispute the recovery.
Incomplete recovery submissions: missing documents that are required by the treaty but not tracked by the claims team.
Recovery claims submitted on a different premium basis than the treaty was written on, generating disputes about the proportion recoverable.
No systematic tracking of outstanding recovery amounts, leading to under-reporting of the reinsurance asset in the statutory financial returns.
Failure to account for recoveries in the claims reserve, overstating the net claims liability and understating the technical result.

blocks.h: The operational function responsible for receiving, assessing, investigating, and settling claims made by or on behalf of policyholders under the terms of their life assurance policies.

The documentary evidence submitted to the insurer to establish that the life assured has died. In Nigeria, the primary document is the National Population Commission death certificate, supported by a medical certificate of cause of death.
A formal legal inquiry conducted by a coroner into the circumstances and cause of a sudden, unexplained, violent, or suspicious death. Inquest findings may affect the insurer’s claims assessment.

A policy exclusion that limits the insurer’s liability to a return of premiums where death by suicide occurs within the first 12 to 24 months of the policy. After the exclusion period, the full sum assured is payable.

A legal status declared by a court in respect of a missing person who has been continuously absent and unheard of for the statutory period (typically seven years under the Nigerian Evidence Act). A declaration of presumed death enables a life assurance claim to proceed.

A claim made by a policyholder on the expiry of the defined policy term of an endowment or savings policy, where the life assured is still alive. The insurer is obligated to pay the maturity sum assured and any accumulated bonuses.

A periodic payment made under a money-back plan to a policyholder who is alive on a defined anniversary date during the policy term. Survival benefits are a scheduled contractual entitlement, not discretionary.

A lump-sum benefit payable upon the diagnosis of a specified dread disease (such as cancer, myocardial infarction, or stroke) that meets the policy’s clinical definition, provided the policyholder survives the survival period.

A condition in which the policyholder is, due to illness or injury, permanently and totally unable to engage in any occupation for which they are reasonably qualified, or their own specific occupation, depending on the policy definition.
The minimum period (typically 14–30 days) a policyholder must survive after the diagnosis of a critical illness before the CI benefit becomes payable.

A claim that involves deliberate misrepresentation, fabrication of evidence, or concealment of material facts, designed to obtain a benefit payment to which the claimant is not entitled under the true facts of the case.
A dedicated team within the claims function responsible for investigating claims where fraud indicators are present. The SIU operates independently of the claims approval function.
A payment made by the insurer without legal obligation and without admission of liability, as a gesture of goodwill. Requires senior management approval and specific governance documentation.
Life assurance benefit proceeds that the insurer is unable to pay because the policyholder or beneficiary cannot be located after documented tracing efforts.
A NAICOM-administered central repository to which life insurers must remit unclaimed benefit proceeds that remain outstanding after the prescribed statutory period.

A principle of insurance contract interpretation under which ambiguities in policy wording are construed against the party that drafted the document, typically the insurer. This principle requires the insurer to resolve genuinely ambiguous policy terms in the claimant’s favour.
The insurer’s right to treat a policy as void from inception (ab initio) where material non-disclosure or misrepresentation by the proposer is established. The effect is that no claim is payable.
